name: Ben Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the sports reporter on the Gazette, the regional daily, and my main job is covering the town's football club, which plays in the fourth tier. Match days I'm in the press box with a laptop and a pie, writing the live updates and then the report, and on weekdays I'm at training, ringing the manager and doing the grassroots stuff, school finals, the women's league, the darts. I've done it five years and I know every steward by name. What wears me out is evenings and weekends, I haven't had a free Saturday since I was twenty-two.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Does AI come into your work at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Not mine. The Gazette started running computer-written results for the Sunday leagues last year, just scores dropped into a template, and I'll admit nobody complained. I write my own stuff, I don't even use the spell checker much. I live on my own in a rented flat near the ground, my mum and dad are ten minutes away, and I've got maybe two months of money put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there you go, told you, you still need someone in the press box. I'd probably say it to the other reporters at the match, half joking. I wouldn't post about it, I don't really post opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it doesn't make me feel that safe. Print has been losing money for years. The sports desk at the Gazette, my paper, was four people when I joined and it's two now. AI or not, the next cut could be me or Gary, and Gary's been there twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal, same club, same patch. I'd try to put a bit more aside each month, maybe fifty quid more, because two months isn't much. I'd keep my contacts at the club warm, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, if I'm honest. Nothing to do with robots, it's just the paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by keeping your contacts warm, just in case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The club's media officer, Lewis, is leaving next year, and I've wondered about that job more than once. It's less writing and more filming interviews and running the club's social media. I'd hate leaving the paper, but at least the club isn't shrinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the paper made a cut tomorrow, who'd go, you or Gary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably me, because Gary's got the redundancy rights and the editor likes him. I'd have two months and my mum's spare room. I don't love saying that at twenty-seven, but that's the truth.

say: You still need someone in the **press box**, AI or not.
I'd say it half joking at the match, but I **wouldn't post** opinions online.
think: The **sports desk** has already shrunk from four people to two.
The next cut could be me or Gary, and I'd likely be **first**.
do: Carry on covering the **same club** and the grassroots patch.
Save about **fifty pounds more** each month.
Keep in touch with the club's **media officer** about his job.
feel: **Uneasy** about the **paper's money**, not about robots.
S0.quote: The sports desk at the Gazette, my paper, was four people when I joined and it's two now.
fieldNote: His worry comes from the **print decline**, and the plateau doesn't touch it.
Thinks he'd be cut **before Gary** because of length of service, and says so plainly.
Has a quiet **fallback** in the club's media officer job, though he'd hate to leave the paper.

steps.text: Keep covering the fourth-tier club and grassroots sport
Put an extra fifty pounds a month into savings
Keep in touch with Lewis about the club media officer job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can write the Sunday league scores but it can't tell you why a manager looked gutted in the tunnel. At work I'd keep my head down and do the job. I'm not one for big statements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I reckon a lot of my weekday work goes. Rewriting the club's press releases, the transfer rumours, the league tables and the previews, a machine could knock those out. The match report, the interviews, the being there, maybe that's left, but that's half a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be honest, I'd probably wait and see for the first few months and hope it doesn't hit sport as hard. I'd keep saving the extra fifty a month and stop going out after matches with the lads as much. If the club job came up I'd go for it properly this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Stomach-knotted worried. I'm not good with this sort of change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. If the editor asked you to start using the AI tools, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do it, grudgingly, because I'm not going to lose my job over a principle. But I'd be slow at it. I'd be the old slow one with the AI tools at twenty-seven, and the younger reporters would be quicker than me. That bothers me more than I'd admit at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, oddly, even though he's safer on paper. He's fifty-two and he's never done anything else. If they turned sport into a one-man job with a machine, I don't know where he'd go.

say: AI can write **Sunday league scores**, but it can't read a manager's face in the **tunnel**.
At work I'd **keep my head down** and just do the job.
think: Most of my **weekday work**, like press releases and previews, would go.
What's left is **half a job**: match reports, interviews and being there.
do: **Wait and see** for a few months before changing anything.
Keep saving the **extra fifty** and cut back on nights out after matches.
Apply properly for the **club media job** if it comes up.
feel: **Stomach-knotted** worry, and fear of being the **slow one**.
S1.quote: I'd be the old slow one with the AI tools at twenty-seven, and the younger reporters would be quicker than me.
fieldNote: Sees his job shrinking to **half a job** and himself as the likely one cut.
His instinct is to **wait and see**, but he admits he'd use the tools rather than lose the job.
Worries about **Gary**, the older colleague, even though Gary looks safer on paper.

steps.text: Hold off on changes for a few months and watch the sports desk
Cut nights out with the lads after matches
Apply for the club media officer job when Lewis leaves

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad, and nobody asked for it. I'd probably agree with whatever most people at work were saying. I'm not going to march about it, but I'd sign a petition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm finished at the Gazette in two years. If a machine can do any thinking work, it can write a match report from the TV feed and the stats, and the paper would jump at that. Robots are three years behind, but my job's barely hands-on anyway, unless you count carrying a laptop up the press box stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the club media officer job straight away, because filming and being at the ground is the closest thing to hands-on I've got, and that buys me a few years. I'd cut right back, no holidays, no new phone. If I lost the job I'd move back in with my mum and dad for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky, if I'm honest. Two months of savings doesn't feel like much at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum and dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, can I have my old room back for a bit, and I'd feel about fifteen saying it. Dad would say yes before I'd finished. He drove buses for thirty years, he'd just tell me to get my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said panicky, but you also have a plan. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. My plan is moving back to my old bedroom at my mum and dad's and hoping the football club hires me. That's a soft landing, not a plan.

say: It's mad and **nobody asked** for it.
I'd sign a **petition**, but I'm not going to march about it.
think: I'm probably **finished at the Gazette** within two years.
Robots lag three years, but my job is **barely hands-on** anyway.
do: Go for the **club media officer** job straight away.
Cut out **holidays** and a new phone.
Move back in with my **parents** if I lose the job.
feel: **Panicky**, because **two months** of savings feels like nothing.
S2.quote: My plan is moving back to my old bedroom at my mum and dad's and hoping the football club hires me. That's a soft landing, not a plan.
fieldNote: Expects to **lose his job** within two years, with a thin two-month cushion.
Sees the club role, with filming and **being at the ground**, as buying time before robots.
His **parents' spare room** is his real safety net, and he's embarrassed by it.

steps.text: Apply for the club media officer job straight away
Cancel this year's holiday and keep the old phone
Move back into his old room at his parents' house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, at least. People can get ready. I'd probably say to the lads at five-a-side that we should all be thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the Gazette sports job still goes, just around 2031 instead of 2028. Five years gives me time to get into the club and learn the video side, which leans a bit more on being there. The robots in 2034 would get that too eventually, but that's eight years off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do a short video editing course at the college, evenings. I'd get the club job when Lewis leaves, or something like it at another club. And I'd keep saving, aiming for four months instead of two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed underneath, but less of a panic. I can see the steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you don't like new things. Would you really do the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to make myself. If I've got five years' warning and I just sit there, that's on me. My dad would have something to say about it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be hardest about leaving the paper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The byline, honestly. Seeing my name on the back page of the paper every Monday still gives me a buzz. Working for the football club, I'd just be the club's voice. Not my own any more.

say: Five years is **something**, at least; people can **get ready**.
I'd tell the lads at **five-a-side** we should all be thinking about it.
think: The Gazette sports job still goes, just around **2031** instead of 2028.
Five years lets me move into the club's **video side**, which leans on being there.
do: Take an evening **video editing** course at the college.
Move into the **club media job** or something like it.
Build savings from two months to **four**.
feel: Still **alarmed** underneath, but less **panic** because the steps are visible.
S3.quote: Seeing my name on the back page of the paper every Monday still gives me a buzz. Working for the football club, I'd just be the club's voice.
fieldNote: Still expects to **lose the paper job**; the time only changes how he leaves.
Thinks about the **robot timeline** for his next job, which buys him a few more years.
Losing his **byline** matters to him as much as the money.

steps.text: Take an evening video editing course at the local college
Move to the club media officer job when it opens
Build savings from two months to four months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time in football, never mind tech. I'd probably shrug in public. Nobody plans ten years ahead in sport.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years means I can keep doing the job I love for a good while. I'd be thirty-seven when it comes. That's old enough to have moved into something steadier, maybe the club, maybe a league office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at the Gazette for a few years and not change much. I'd keep up the extra saving. Somewhere in there I'd try to move to the club side, but I'd probably leave it later than I should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but not lying awake. It's a slow worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd leave it later than you should. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's me. I didn't learn to drive till I was twenty-four because I kept putting it off. I know I'd put off this change too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably seeing Gary go, or someone I know at another paper. Once it's a real face, I move. Until then I tell myself there's time.

Nobody **plans ten years ahead** in sport, so I'd shrug in public.
think: I can keep doing the **job I love** for a good while.
At **thirty-seven** I'd want to be somewhere steadier, like the club or a league office.
do: Keep going at the **Gazette** for a few years without big changes.
Keep up the **extra saving** each month.
Try to move to the **club side**, probably later than I should.
feel: **Anxious**, but it's a **slow worry**, not a sleepless one.
S4.quote: I didn't learn to drive till I was twenty-four because I kept putting it off. I know I'd put off this change too.
fieldNote: Admits his **resistance** openly and predicts he'd move too late.
Says he only acts once a **real colleague** goes, which is useful about how he works.
Still sees his **job ending** eventually, so the worry stays real despite the long runway.

steps.text: Keep covering the club for the Gazette for a few years
Keep saving fifty pounds extra each month
Wait to move to the club until a colleague is cut

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no contest. I've got two months saved, no other trade, and I'd be the first one out at the Gazette. What would help is decent notice and some money to retrain, maybe a course in video or club media paid for by someone other than me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the fans. If every match report is written by a machine, I think the fans would notice, even if the newspaper owners didn't. Then do people still care about the paper?

headlineQuote: If every match report is written by a machine, I think the fans would notice, even if the newspaper owners didn't.
portrait: Ben is a **27-year-old** sports reporter on a regional daily, covering a **fourth-tier** football club.
He never uses AI, lives alone near the ground, and has about **two months** saved.
He already fears being cut **before Gary**, the long-serving colleague, as print sport shrinks.
He tends to **wait**, with his **parents' spare room** as his real safety net.
His escape route is the **club media job**, which he'd move to faster as AGI gets closer.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with two months saved and no other **trade**.
whatWouldHelp: **Decent notice** and paid **retraining**, maybe in video or club media.
